Empirical Research Plan:  Texas AP Incentive Program and Student Outcomes  

-------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
-------------------------------------------------
Chosen method:  Staggered Difference-in-Differences (DID) complemented by an event-study specification.

Why appropri­ate:  
• The cash–for-scores program was rolled out to different high schools in different years; some campuses never joined.  
• We observe multiple pre- and post-years for each school and for multiple cohorts of students.  
• The policy shock is at the school-year level, but outcomes are at the student level, allowing rich fixed-effects and covariate adjustment.  
• An event-study around the adoption year lets us test the parallel-trends assumption and visualize dynamics.  
• RDD is inappropriate because the score cut-off (3,4,5) defines payment on the outcome itself, not ex-ante eligibility. IV is unnecessary given the clean policy timing.

-------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  
-------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
  Treat_i = 1 if student i attends high school s in year t when the AP Incentive Program is active on that campus; 0 otherwise.

Control group (counterfactual)  
  Students in schools that have not yet adopted or never adopt in the same calendar year.

Treatment timing (event date)  
  Adoption_s = the first academic year the program operates at school s.  
  For the event study we define k = t – Adoption_s (k = 0 is first treated year).

Sample construction (to minimize differential exposure)  
  Keep cohorts whose 9th-grade year is ≤3 years before or ≤3 years after Adoption_s.  

No running variable / cutoff—this is a panel DID, not an RDD.

-------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
-------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel Trends: In the absence of the incentive program, treated and control schools would have evolved similarly in AP take-up and downstream outcomes.  
  • Plausibility: We can condition on rich pre-policy outcomes and demographics and run pre-trend tests.

A2. No Spillovers: A school’s adoption does not affect students in non-adopting schools (e.g., through district re-zoning or peer effects).  
  • Plausibility: Texas high schools draw from stable attendance zones; within-district spillovers are unlikely but will be probed by dropping bordering schools.

A3. No Anticipatory Behavior: Students or administrators did not alter behavior in advance of the exact adoption year.  
  • Plausibility: Grants were typically announced <1 year before implementation; test by including leads in the event study.

A4. Stable Composition: Adoption does not induce non-random student sorting (e.g., high achievers transferring in).  
  • Plausibility: Texas high-school transfer barriers are high; check by comparing baseline demographics and by re-estimating on “stayers” (students present in the same school since 9th grade).

-------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigation  
-------------------------------------------------
T1. Non-random program adoption (selection on time-varying unobservables).  
   Mitigation:  
  • School fixed effects soak up all time-invariant selection.  
  • Include district×year fixed effects to control for common local shocks.  
  • Event-study pre-trends + placebo adoption dates.

T2. Differential trends in accountability pressure or resources.  
   Mitigation:  
  • Control for time-varying school inputs (per-pupil spending, teacher-student ratio).  
  • Triple-difference with middle schools in the same feeder pattern as an additional counterfactual.

T3. Measurement error in adoption year.  
   Mitigation:  
  • Cross-validate TEA program files with foundation grant dates.  
  • Drop ambiguous adopters, re-estimate.

-------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline  
-------------------------------------------------
```r
# -------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# -------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)      # fast fixed-effect regressions
library(did)         # Callaway-Sant’Anna estimator
library(broom)       # tidy outputs

# -------------------------------------------
# 1. Data Loading
# -------------------------------------------
students   <- read_csv("TX_students.csv")      # student-level panel
schools    <- read_csv("TX_school_covs.csv")   # time-varying school info
adoptions  <- read_csv("APIP_adoption.csv")    # school, first_treated_year

# -------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable Construction
# -------------------------------------------
df <- students %>% 
      left_join(adoptions, by = "school_id") %>%
      left_join(schools,   by = c("school_id","year")) %>%
      mutate( treat = ifelse(!is.na(first_treated_year) & 
                             year >= first_treated_year, 1, 0),
              years_since = year - first_treated_year,
              cohort9 = ifelse(grade==9, year, NA) %>% 
                        ave(., student_id, FUN=function(x) x[!is.na(x)][1]),
              post = treat,
              outcome_AP_take   = as.numeric(AP_exam_taken),
              outcome_AP_pass   = as.numeric(AP_score>=3),
              outcome_grad      = as.numeric(graduated_hs),
              outcome_college   = as.numeric(enrolled_college))

# Restrict to ±3 cohorts
df <- df %>% filter(cohort9 >= first_treated_year-3 &
                    cohort9 <= first_treated_year+3)

# -------------------------------------------
# 3. Main DID Specification
# -------------------------------------------
did_main <- feols(outcome_AP_take ~ post + 
                  i(year) +                    # year FE
                  i(school_id) +               # school FE
                  gender + race + frpl +       # student covariates
                  per_pupil_spend +            # time-varying school covs
                  grade,                       # grade FE
                  cluster = ~school_id,
                  data = df)

summary(did_main)

# -------------------------------------------
# 4. Event-Study (Sun & Abraham, staggered)
# -------------------------------------------
df <- df %>% mutate(event_time = years_since)

es <- feols(outcome_AP_take ~ sunab(first_treated_year, year) + 
            i(school_id) + i(year) + gender + race + frpl,
            cluster = ~school_id,
            data = df)

iplot(es)   # visual pre-trend check

# -------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness Check: Remove schools that adopt in 1st or last year
# -------------------------------------------
adopt_counts <- adoptions %>% 
                filter(first_treated_year %in% range(df$year)) %>% 
                pull(school_id)

df_rb <- df %>% filter(!school_id %in% adopt_counts)

did_rb <- feols(outcome_AP_take ~ post + i(year) + i(school_id),
                cluster=~school_id,
                data = df_rb)

etable(did_main, did_rb, se="cluster")
```

-------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  
-------------------------------------------------
Economic intuition and prior descriptive work suggest positive effects:  
• AP exam participation: +5–8 percentage points (pp) off a baseline of ~25 pp.  
• Passing (score ≥ 3): +2–3 pp.  
• High-school graduation: +1 pp.  
• Immediate college enrollment: +2 pp.  
Magnitude rationale: cash incentives ($100 per 3-plus score) combined with teacher rewards meaningfully raise salience and resources but do not overhaul the entire curriculum.

-------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable)  

C1 Parallel pre-trends visually verified ………………… 0.8  
C2 No simultaneous confounding policies ……………… 0.7  
C3 No spillovers / SUTVA holds …………………………… 0.7  
C4 Stable unit composition ………………………………… 0.8  
C5 Treatment timing exogenous to time-varying shocks … 0.6  

Overall, while reasonably strong, the design hinges on successful pre-trend tests and robustness to school-level selection.
